Dense data pulling against decision speed

Type, hierarchy and colour set for the worst-case viewing moment
Configurable pages built from widgets

Analyse returns, attribution and risk across asset classes

Client, phase two

journey.line: Helen Marsh · Portfolio Manager · Asset manager, London · Quarterly board pack, one afternoon
journey.scenario: Helen is preparing a quarterly board meeting. She opens Fusion to pull performance, attribution and risk for the book, slices by asset class and period, and builds the view she will present live while the numbers are still updating.
journey.goal: Walk into the board meeting with numbers she trusts, built in one surface, without a spreadsheet detour.
approachText: Refine the view, back to filters
Phase two reuses the same screens

phases.title: Build the view
phases.description: Cube, filters and widgets in one surface

steps.title: Find the data
steps.description: Helen selects the data cube for her book. FactSet's engine feeds it, so the shape of the data is fixed and the first useful view has to be fast.
steps.backstage: FactSet engine returns the cube. The shape of the data is fixed, so the first view has to be fast.

steps.title: Shape the view
steps.description: Filter and slice: asset class, period, benchmark. The old RaaS layout couldn't flex to different data or roles.
recommendations: Comparison tools tailored to data complexity and role
steps.backstage: Salt filter bar and toggles. Entitlements decide which options each person sees.

steps.title: Analyse
steps.description: Returns, attribution and risk across asset classes, in widgets that work across cubes and permission levels.
recommendations: Data tables and chart frames on Salt
steps.backstage: One widget shell renders a table or a chart from the same data contract, across cubes.

steps.title: Present
steps.description: She presents the screen live, under pressure. Type, hierarchy and colour were set for this moment, not the clean demo.
recommendations: Board-ready report without leaving the surface
Worst-case viewing moment as the baseline
steps.backstage: Dashboard page configuration saved per user. Accessibility specialist reviews before release.

steps.title: Share and reuse
steps.description: Phase two: the same screens reach external clients who had no training. One codebase, entitlement decides what each person sees.
recommendations: Same patterns for internal and external users
Patterns reused across other Fusion modules
steps.backstage: One codebase. Entitlement-based views for clients. Import and export through FactSet.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: Get in front of end users directly and earlier. The start leaned on product-owner requirements. Ship a leaner version one with fewer modules, and bring the accessibility specialist in from week one.

takeaways.label: Insight
takeaways.text: Their real need was trust in the numbers, not more features. The middle configuration tier added choices without changing what people built, so it went.

takeaways.label: Who was in the room
takeaways.text: A product owner setting requirements, a UX designer shared across projects, engineering in daily stand-ups, an accessibility specialist in every review, and FactSet behind the data.

takeaways.label: How I measure it
takeaways.text: Zero WCAG AA violations at ship. Widget and filtering patterns reused across other Fusion modules. Phase two opened the product to external clients, and several signed after that launch.

decisions.title: Dashboard structure

choices.label: Fixed layouts per report type
transcript: Fixed layout. New data cube = new page.

decisions.reason: We explored fixed layouts per report type and a widget grid. Fixed layouts were faster to ship, but every new data cube would have needed a new page. The grid won because one widget serves many cubes and permission levels.
decisions.tradeoff: Slower to ship than fixed layouts, and every widget had to earn its place in one of the four workflow steps.
decisions.outcome: Widget and filtering patterns reused across other Fusion modules.

decisions.title: Configuration
decisions.reason: Early versions had three levels of configuration. Testing showed the middle tier added cognitive load without changing what people built. I removed it. The test I use for what not to design: is this serving a real workflow contradiction, or one team's preference?
decisions.tradeoff: Fewer options for power users who liked the middle tier.
decisions.outcome: The first useful view was faster to reach.

decisions.title: Phase two
decisions.reason: Phase two brought in clients who'd had no training. We chose one product with entitlement-based views over a simplified client version, so patterns stayed consistent and the team kept one codebase.
decisions.tradeoff: Client constraints live in the same codebase as the internal views.
decisions.outcome: Clients onboarded with no training, and several signed after the phase two launch.

personas.intro: My two design personas: a designer like me and the developer who inspects the output. Role-based working assumptions the private alpha exists to test, not research participants.

items.name: Mei Lin
items.role:
Product Designer
Works inside a design system

groups.label: Goals
items: Prompt, generate, compare, tune, export
See the same screen in Salt, Material, Fluent and Carbon
Stay in control without making the AI useless

groups.label: Frictions
items: Designing for output you can't predict
Designing for yourself hides your blind spots
Free-form generated UI looked impressive and was unusable

groups.label: In this app
items: A compare step across systems
Tune density, theme and charts
Official components only, never overridden

items.name: Dev Patel
items.quote: “Show me code I recognise, not a picture of a screen.”

groups.label: Goals
items: Inspect the exported React
Recognise each system's official components
Close the gap between a Figma file and code

groups.label: Frictions
items: Generated screens that use none of the team's components
Screens nobody tested with a user
A Figma file with nothing to inspect

groups.label: In this app
items: Export React a developer recognises
Each system's published React components
Token mapping underneath, mapped not generated

journey.line: Mei Lin · Product Designer · Works inside a design system · One screen in Salt, a Material version due, one afternoon
journey.scenario: Mei has a screen to design in Salt by Friday and a Material version due for a sister team. She describes the screen, lets the model draft it from official components, compares the systems, tunes density and theme, and exports React a developer can inspect.
journey.goal: Reach a useful, inspectable screen in a real design system without rebuilding it by hand for every system.
approachText: Alpha feedback changes the compare step
quotes: “That is a draft, not an answer.”
“I would never ship the first answer.”
“Does it work without me guiding it?”

phases.title: Draft
phases.description: Prompt and generate from official components

steps.title: Prompt
steps.description: Mei describes the screen in words. The output can't be fully predicted, so the prompt has to say what matters: system, density, data.
recommendations: Name the system and density in the prompt
steps.backstage: The prompt is read with the system, density and data named, so the draft starts inside the right constraints.

steps.title: Generate
steps.description: The model drafts the screen from the system's official React components. Free-form UI looked impressive and was unusable.
recommendations: The first answer is a draft
steps.backstage: Claude drafts the screen from the system's official React components. Free-form drawing is never allowed.

steps.title: Compare systems
steps.description: The same screen in Salt, Material, Fluent and Carbon. The hard part is where the systems disagree.
recommendations: Strictest definition wins on a disagreement
steps.backstage: Token mapping holds five systems in one structure. Where two systems disagree, the strictest definition wins.

steps.title: Tune
steps.description: Density, theme and charts. This is where the person decides, and where Mei corrects the model most often.
recommendations: Compare and tune before anything exports
steps.backstage: Density, theme and chart props re-render the same component tree. Nothing is redrawn by hand.

steps.title: Export React
steps.description: Code a developer recognises. It closes the gap between a Figma file and the thing a developer can inspect.
steps.backstage: React export with the component tree and tokens a developer can inspect. It does not ship the product.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: The next validation question: can another designer reach a useful, inspectable screen without me guiding them? The private alpha exists to answer it, and to break my own assumptions.

takeaways.label: Insight
takeaways.text: Free-form generated UI looked impressive and was unusable. Official components only, never overridden, gave output a developer recognises at the cost of the model having fewer moves.

takeaways.label: Who was in the room
takeaways.text: Me, solo. Claude as the drafting model. A developer inspecting the export as the test of whether a screen is real. Designers like me as the first users, which is the trap the alpha exists to check.

takeaways.label: How I measure it
takeaways.text: No adoption rate, time saving or external testing result is claimed. What I watch: screens that export without a hand rebuild, and how often I correct the model at the compare and tune steps.

decisions.title: Generation

choices.label: Official components only, never overridden
transcript: Every element maps to a published component

choices.label: Letting the model draw free-form UI
transcript: Looks impressive, nothing a developer can ship

decisions.reason: We explored letting the model draw free-form UI and restricting it to each system's published React components. Free-form looked impressive and was unusable. Official-only won. The output is something a developer recognises, at the cost of the model having fewer moves.
decisions.tradeoff: The model has fewer moves, so some layouts it could draw are off the table.
decisions.outcome: The output is something a developer recognises and can inspect.

decisions.title: Switching systems

choices.label: Five systems, one model underneath
transcript: Switch system, density or theme without a hand rebuild

decisions.reason: I mapped their tokens, density scales and theming into one structure so a screen can switch system without being rebuilt by hand. The hard part was where the systems disagree, and I chose the strictest definition each time.
decisions.tradeoff: The strictest definition wins, so a looser system loses some of its own defaults.
decisions.outcome: Switch system, density or theme and the screen rebuilds without a hand rebuild.

decisions.title: Export

choices.label: Compare and tune before export
transcript: The person decides where the systems disagree

choices.label: The model's first answer
transcript: The model's guess ships as it came, and the person corrects it in code

decisions.reason: The model's first answer is a draft. The flow forces a compare step across systems and a tune step on the screen before anything exports. That's where the person decides, and where I correct the model most often.
decisions.tradeoff: Nothing exports from the first answer. The flow is slower by design.
decisions.outcome: The compare and tune steps are where the person decides, and where I correct the model most often.

personas.intro: Three users, one star: the child who ticks, the parent who sets it up, and the second adult who never opted in. Composite roles from the case, not research participants.

items.name: Leo, 6
items.role:
The child
Can't read much yet
items.quote: Knows his own name, his colour and his football.

groups.label: Wants
items: To tick it himself
See the star land
Find out what the pet turns into

groups.label: Breaks when
items: A word he can't read is in the way
A tap target is small
A missed day makes the week feel lost

groups.label: Design answer
items: A big illustrated banner per theme
Celebration on every tick
A weekly pet so one bad day doesn't end the game

items.name: The parent
items.role:
Sets it up
Decides in two minutes if it stays
items.quote: Downloads it after another bedtime argument.

groups.label: Wants
items: Routines done without nagging
One place both adults can see
Nothing that sells to her kids

groups.label: Breaks when
items: Setup takes more than a minute
An ad appears
The app hands the phone to the child with no guard rails

groups.label: Design answer
items: A sample family on first open, so value shows before any setup
Kid Mode and a parental gate
Custom activities, so Mandarin sits next to teeth

items.name: The second adult
items.role:
Never opted in
Partner, grandparent, childminder
items.quote: Got an invite on WhatsApp. Has thirty seconds.

groups.label: Wants
items: To tick a star
Get back to bedtime

groups.label: Breaks when
items: Any learning
A board that looks different from the one the kids know

groups.label: Design answer
items: Invite to the same board
Same screen, same stars
From their own phone

journey.line: The parent · Sets it up · Two children, two adults · From a bad bedtime to week two, with Leo, 6, underneath
journey.scenario: After another bad bedtime the parent downloads Winking Star, finds the Sample Family already set up, hands the phone to Leo for the first tick, and by the end of the week a Mystery Pet has grown and grandma has joined the board.
journey.goal: Routines done without nagging, a child who asks to tick his own stars, and a second adult on the same board.
approachText: Weekly loop, a new egg on Monday
Offline ticks sync on reconnect, from any phone
quotes: “Oh, there is already a family in here.”

phases.title: First week
phases.description: From a bad bedtime to the first reveal

phases.title: Keep coming back
phases.description: The weekly loop and the second adult

steps.title: Another bad bedtime
steps.description: Searches for a chore chart app. Most are checklists, subscriptions or ads. Child feels fed up.
recommendations: Ad-free, kid-first on the store page
steps.backstage: App Store listing in the Kids Category: ad-free, no tracking, privacy manifest.

steps.title: First open
steps.description: Opens the app and finds the Sample Family already set up. Child feels curious.
recommendations: Add your own family when you like it
steps.backstage: Sample Family seeded on first open. No account, no tour, no permission prompt.

steps.title: First tick
steps.description: Hands the phone over. The child taps teeth. A star lands and confetti fires. Child feels delighted.
steps.backstage: The tick writes to the shared board. Celebration fires unless Calm Mode is on.

steps.title: End of day
steps.description: Checks Home. The pet grew a stage. A treasure dropped. Child feels proud, or a bit flat.
recommendations: The pet grows on what was done
steps.backstage: Pet stage computed from the week's stars. A treasure drops. Day rolls over at local midnight.

steps.title: End of week
steps.description: Prints the weekly summary for the fridge. Monday, a new pet arrives. Child feels excited.
recommendations: Old pet joins the Pet Pals collection
steps.backstage: Weekly summary printed. A new egg on Monday; the old pet joins Pet Pals.

steps.title: Second adult joins
steps.description: Invites grandma to the board. She opens it and ticks a bath. Child feels relieved, and a bit smug.
steps.backstage: Invite link joins the same board. Offline ticks queue and sync on reconnect through Firebase.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: The pet card still truncates its helper text at the smallest sizes, and the pet family labels are not translated yet. Both found in my own usability pass and on the list.

takeaways.label: Insight
takeaways.text: The checklist lost in our own house within a week. Big icons, sticker mechanics, bright colour and celebration moments won, and a weekly pet means one bad day does not end the game.

takeaways.label: Who was in the room
takeaways.text: Built for my own two kids first and watched them use it every evening. A second adult who never opted in. App Store Kids Category rules shaped the parental gate and the privacy manifest.

takeaways.label: How I measure it
takeaways.text: Routines completed per week, weeks retained, and whether a second adult joins the board. Live at 1.0.4 on iPhone and iPad, four releases since launch, five languages.

decisions.title: Daily motivation

choices.label: Stars and a pet
transcript: Tap a routine, a star lands
Research with five to seven year olds
Big icons, stickers and celebration win. A star you can tap beats a box you tick.
Each tap is a small win the child can see
Stars count towards the weekly pet, so the board has a reason to fill up.

choices.label: A plain tick list
transcript: Reads like homework. Nothing happens when the list is done, so the child stops caring by Wednesday.

decisions.reason: Explored a plain tick list. Research on five to seven year olds said big icons, stickers and celebration win. The checklist lost in our own house within a week.
decisions.tradeoff: More art and motion to build and keep consistent: fourteen banners and four pet stages.
decisions.outcome: Routines ticked without nagging in our own house.

decisions.title: First open

choices.label: A sample family before any setup
transcript: The first screen is a full week for a family that already exists. You see what the app does, then swap in your own kids.
A week of routines and stars

choices.label: A tour and an empty state
transcript: Routines live here. Tap to add one when you are ready.
A tour and an empty state
Both ask parents to invest before they have seen the loop. An empty board says nothing about why a child would care.
Add a child before anything shows
No pet, no stars, no week to look at

decisions.reason: Explored a tour and an empty state. Both asked parents to invest before they'd seen the loop. The Sample Family shows a full week on first open, and you replace it when you're ready.
decisions.tradeoff: First-run sample data has to be replaced, so there is a clear swap step.

decisions.title: Access and trust

choices.label: Lifetime unlock
transcript: Free to start, one payment if you want everything. No ads, no third-party tracking.
Their kids are not the product

choices.label: A small subscription
transcript: Recurring revenue, and a recurring reason to distrust the app. Every renewal is a chance to feel tricked.
A trial that turns into a charge
A paywall between a child and their pet

decisions.reason: It's for children, and trust is the product. Free to start, one payment if you want everything, no ads, no third-party tracking.
decisions.outcome: Free to start, one payment if you want everything, no ads, no third-party tracking.

decisions.title: A theme per child

choices.label: A theme per child, drawn not templated
transcript: Fourteen illustrated banners, from Football and Dinosaur to Ocean, Unicorn and Robot, plus a photo avatar if they want their own face on it.
Colour and picture before they can read

choices.label: One look for all
transcript: Cheaper to build and keep consistent. Every card is the same grey, so a six year old cannot tell which one is theirs.
Kids need a parent to point at their card

decisions.reason: Explored one look for all. Kids find their own card by colour and picture before they can read. Fourteen illustrated banners, from Football and Dinosaur to Ocean, Unicorn and Robot, plus a photo avatar if they want their own face on it.
decisions.tradeoff: Fourteen illustrated banners to draw and keep consistent.
decisions.outcome: Kids find their own card by colour and picture before they can read.

decisions.title: A parental gate

choices.label: A quick maths question gates the exits
transcript: A speed bump, not a lock
A sum a seven year old cannot guess and a parent does not need to remember. It only guards edits, so there is nothing to forget.

choices.label: A PIN, or a locked app
transcript: A PIN, or a locked app
Parents forget PINs and kids watch them type. A locked app also locks the parent out of a quick edit at bedtime.

decisions.reason: Explored a PIN. Parents forget PINs and kids watch them type. A quick maths question gates anything that leaves the app, uploads a photo or deletes an account, and Kid Mode locks editing so the phone can be handed over mid-routine.
decisions.tradeoff: A maths question is a speed bump for parents too.
decisions.outcome: Kid Mode lets the phone be handed over mid-routine.

decisions.title: Weekly pet

choices.label: A weekly pet with four stages
transcript: Stars count up and never down. One missed bath does not end the week, and Monday always brings a new egg.
A daily number resets at midnight. A pet that grows across the week survives a bad Tuesday.

choices.label: A daily score
transcript: Missed bath and reading. Score reset.
Every missed routine is a loss the child sees at bedtime. The number resets, so a bad day erases a good one.
No reason to try again on Friday

decisions.reason: Daily stars count up and never down. The pet grows across the week on what was done, so one missed bath doesn't end the week, and Monday always brings a new egg.
decisions.tradeoff: No daily pressure means less urgency on a quiet day.
decisions.outcome: One missed bath does not end the week, and Monday always brings a new egg.

personas.intro: Four composite roles from the four teams I sat with for a year: the deal owner who prices, the ops lead who approves, legal who checks the terms, and the product owner who keeps the portfolio. Composite roles, not research participants.
personas.note: Composite roles drawn from a year with the four teams. Not research participants, and no individual is depicted.

items.role:
Custody sales
Prices and defends the deal

Compare iterations without rebuilding the sheet
Know where approval is stuck

Numbers that disagree by team
Approval chased over email

Quick overview per deal
Status and deal lead on the landing page

Reviewing the full sheet for one change

groups.label: In this app

Checks as you go, before approval
Step five writes the sign-off summary

Keep the terms consistent across deals

Changes with no name on them

Product

Load data without hand-keying
Keep the people who love Excel

Hand-keyed portfolios
Migration that loses people

Upload template the system maps
Tiering across AUC and transactions

journey.line: The deal owner · Custody sales · London · Global custody deal, four teams, one platform
journey.scenario: A client asks for a reprice before a call. The deal owner opens the deal, loads the portfolio, builds a new iteration on the benchmark rate card, compares it with the last two, and sends it for approval.
journey.goal: Price the deal in one sitting, know it is within tolerance, and get sign-off with a trail that survives an audit.
approachText: Fix at the field, back to pricing
Upload template brings the last across
quotes: “Will product recognise this as a deal?”
“Do I have to key all this in again?”
“Three versions, so I can say what is wrong.”
“Audit can have this as it is.”

phases.title: Build the deal
phases.description: Create, load and price in one object

steps.title: Create the deal
steps.description: The deal owner creates the deal: name, region, segment, lead. Before, every team set a deal up its own way.
recommendations: Status and deal lead on the landing page
steps.backstage: Deal object created with role-based views. Deal team and status stored once.

steps.title: Load the portfolio
steps.description: Loads holdings and transactions, or uploads the filled template the system maps. Before, hand-keyed from a spreadsheet.
recommendations: Upload template, mapped by the system
steps.backstage: Mapping rules translate the template to the data model. Unmapped columns block the import.

steps.title: Price and iterate
steps.description: Builds iterations on benchmark rate cards. Tolerance checks run as each field changes, not at approval.
steps.backstage: Tolerance rules and benchmark rate cards run on every change.

steps.title: Compare and tier
steps.description: Puts iterations side by side in the compare grid, chooses columns, applies tiering across AUC and transactions.
recommendations: Compare grid with a column chooser
steps.backstage: Grid settings saved per user. Tiering rules by AUC band and transaction type.

steps.title: Approve and sign off
steps.description: Sends for approval. The approver sees what changed. Step five writes the sign-off summary.
steps.backstage: Approver workflow routes by role. History written per iteration.

takeaways.label: Opportunities
takeaways.text: Catch tolerance breaches at the field, not at approval. Make the comparison a view, not a rebuild. Let the tool write the sign-off.

takeaways.label: Insight
takeaways.text: Most of the arguments were about columns, not about the deal. Once each team saw its own view of the same object, the fight went away.

takeaways.label: Who was in the room
takeaways.text: Custody ops, sales, legal and product. Two UX designers, a junior designer, a BA, a researcher, a data analyst, and engineers in every review.

takeaways.label: How I measure it
takeaways.text: Not measured in my time. Two hours to twenty minutes is my estimate. I would measure time to create a deal, iterations per deal and approvals returned.

decisions.title: One object, four views

choices.label: One deal object with role-based views
transcript: One object underneath. The view changes, the deal does not.

decisions.reason: We explored one product per team and one deal object with four views. Most of the arguments were about columns, not about the deal. Once each team saw its own view of the same object, the fight went away.
decisions.tradeoff: Every change to the object needs all four teams in the review, so reviews are slower.
decisions.outcome: The four teams work on the same deal, and the audit trail is one trail.

decisions.title: Three versions, every review

choices.label: Three versions on the table
transcript: Ops: "B, but keep the totals row from A." Legal: "C hides the history."

choices.label: One proposal, sign-off at the end
transcript: Four teams say "fine" in the room and reopen it by email the next week.

decisions.reason: I ran every review with three versions. People said what was wrong instead of saying yes. Sales got the comparison table, legal got the iteration list, because they asked for them in those rooms.
decisions.tradeoff: Three versions is three times the preparation, every review, for a year.
decisions.outcome: Decisions held after the room. Nothing was reopened by email.

decisions.title: A compare grid with a column chooser

choices.label: Configurable compare grid
transcript: Saved per user. Sales keeps the comparison it needs.

choices.label: A fixed comparison report
transcript: Every team rebuilt its own version in Excel anyway.

decisions.reason: Sales rebuilt the comparison in Excel every time because the report never had the right columns. A grid with a column chooser, saved per user, made the comparison a view instead of a rebuild.
decisions.tradeoff: Saved settings per user and more states to design: empty, too many columns, a column that no longer exists.
decisions.outcome: Sales stopped rebuilding comparisons outside the tool.

decisions.title: An upload template, not a forced migration

choices.label: Upload the template, system maps it
transcript: Meet people where they are, then bring them over.

choices.label: Cut everyone over on day one
transcript: Sixty people keep a private copy and the platform becomes the second source of truth.

decisions.reason: Some people kept the spreadsheet. We built an upload template they could fill in, and the system mapped it to the data model. Meet people where they are, then bring them over.
decisions.tradeoff: Two ways in, so the mapping rules had to be maintained alongside the product.
decisions.outcome: The last people came across. If asked about adoption, the template is the answer.

decisions.title: Checks as you go, and the tool writes the sign-off

choices.label: Validation at the field, summary written for you
transcript: Outside tolerance for Tier B (max 15 %). Needs legal sign-off.
Iteration 3 lowers the final bid to 5.00 % on Benchmark 2024 Tier B. Reduction 18 % exceeds tolerance (15 %), flagged for legal review. Change by R. Mensah.
Checks at the field. Nothing waits for approval to be found.

choices.label: Validate at approval
transcript: "Reduction out of tolerance. Please correct and resubmit." Three days later.

decisions.reason: Tolerance breaches used to be found at approval, days later, by email. The flow checks each field as it changes against the rate card and tolerance rules, and step five writes the sign-off summary from what changed.
decisions.tradeoff: The tolerance rules had to live in the product, so they changed whenever the rate cards did.
decisions.outcome: Breaches surfaced at the field. Legal got a trail that comes out of the tool.

decisions.title: Smart pricing, explored

choices.label: Model suggests a tier, the person decides
transcript: Based on 38 similar deals, same region and segment, past two years.
The model drafts, the deal owner decides.
Status · designed with the data analyst, reviewed, not built in my time

choices.label: Hand-priced from rate cards only
transcript: Every iteration starts from a blank grid and a rate card. Experience lives in the deal owner's head, so a new starter prices slower and less consistently.

decisions.reason: At the end we explored training a model on past deals to suggest an iteration, with the deal owner editing or discarding it. Designed with the data analyst and reviewed with the four teams.
decisions.tradeoff: It needs clean historical data, which we were still assembling. The suggestion must never auto-apply.
decisions.outcome: Designed and reviewed, not built in my time. The same pattern I use in uoaui.ai: the model drafts, I decide.
